title: Beyond Magnitude: Leveraging Direction of RLVR Updates for LLM Reasoning
claim: Signed probability change, unlike magnitude-based metrics, reveals a directional shift and identifies critical updates with the fewest replacements.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: metric formulas, histograms, line plot; color-coded by metric
description: Three-panel figure with a consistent color code per metric: green for entropy, orange for KL divergence, blue for log-probability difference. Panel (a) on the left stacks three rounded boxes with each metric's formula. Entropy and KL sit in a dashed gray group labeled 'Measuring the magnitude'. The blue Logp Difference box sits below it, labeled 'Measuring the direction: Base→RLVR'. Panel (b) shows three log-scale histograms comparing RLVR and base responses. The entropy and KL histograms overlap almost completely, marked 'overlap'. The blue histogram is visibly shifted, with an arrow from 'Base' to 'RLVR'. Panel (c) is a line plot of AIME24 accuracy against token replacement ratio. The blue curve rises fastest and reaches the dashed RLVR line first, circled with a dashed diamond. Entropy, KL and random curves lag behind. An italic blue annotation states the conclusion.
caption: (a) Token-level metrics for analyzing RLVR updates. (b) Histograms of each metric on responses generated by base and RLVR models. With a log-scale y-axis, most values concentrate near zero for all metrics, but only $\Delta \log p$ shows a directional shift distinguishing RLVR from the base model. (c) Token‑replacement performance: replacing base tokens with RLVR choices at positions selected by each metric, where $\Delta \log p$ recovers RLVR performance with the fewest replacements.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models. While existing analyses identify that RLVR-induced changes are sparse, they primarily focus on the **magnitude** of these updates, largely overlooking their **direction**. In this work, we argue that the direction of updates is a more critical lens for understanding RLVR's effects, which can be captured by the signed, token-level log probability difference $\Delta\log p$ between the base and final RLVR models. Through statistical analysis and token-replacement interventions, we demonstrate that $\Delta\log p$ more effectively identifies sparse, yet reasoning-critical updates than magnitude-based metrics (e.g., divergence or entropy). Building on this insight, we propose two practical applications: (1) a *test-time extrapolation* method that amplifies the policy along the learned $\Delta\log p$ direction to improve reasoning accuracy without further training; (2) a *training-time reweighting* method that focuses learning on low-probability (corresponding to higher $\Delta\log p$) tokens, which improves reasoning performance across models and benchmarks. Our work establishes the direction of change as a key principle for analyzing and improving RLVR.
